newsitem.title: FRANCE: New TV committee to promote French language.
newsitem.headline: New TV committee to promote French language.

text.p: French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette, likening the world's television screens to a cultural and economic battlefield, set up a committee on Monday to marshal a French offensive against English-language domination.

The 10-member committee is due to guide creation of state-controlled Tele France International, a channel sometimes described as a French rival to U.S. network CNN or a "showcase for France" that Paris hopes will come on the air in 1998.
Inaugurating the committee, de Charette said France faced a "battle of capital importance" and that Paris risked "decline of the French language" and "loss of markets" unless it took decisive steps.
The new channel aims to project French influence abroad and counter fears that France is being swamped by U.S. culture, ranging from Hollywood movies to hamburgers.

"We are in a world threatened by a unified culture and ways of thinking," de Charette said in an interview with the daily Le Monde coinciding with the launch of the committee. He did not mention America or English by name.
"A great televisual battle is taking place, both on the technological level and on the level of the political, economic and cultural presence of France in the world," he said.
"The outcome of this battle will depend on our ability to be present on screens everywhere in the world," he said.
He said it would be wrong to mimic CNN and that France also needed to "seduce people who neither speak nor understand our language". One solution was to supply images allowing foreign subtitles.

The head of Tele France International, Jean-Paul Cluzel, is due to hand proposals to the committee by mid-1997. In turn, de Charette will make proposals to Prime Minister Alain Juppe in the latter half of the year.

The French state controls 51 percent of Tele France International. Public television stations control the rest, split between France Television with 37 percent, La Sept-Arte and La Cinquieme with eight percent and RFO four percent.
